name: Tughril Beg Enters Baghdad, Seljuk Power at its Peak
summary: Tughril Beg, the Seljuk sultan, enters Baghdad, expels the Shia Buyid dynasty, and receives the title Sultan from the Abbasid Caliph al-Qaim. The Seljuks present themselves as champions of Sunni orthodoxy, rescuing the caliph from Shia dominance. The arrangement mirrors the Buyid period: the sultan holds real power while the caliph provides religious legitimacy. Tughril's successors (Alp Arslan, Malik Shah) build the largest Sunni power since the early Abbasids.

_quarry.structural_significance: The Seljuk conquest of Baghdad creates a new Sunni-Turkic imperial model that shapes the Islamic world for centuries; the sultan-caliph separation of power (military authority vs. religious legitimacy) becomes the template for subsequent Islamic states; the Seljuks' patronage of madrasas (including the Nizamiyya in Baghdad) institutionalizes Sunni religious education; their defeat by the Mongols (1243 at Köse Dağ) is the first step toward the later Mongol destruction of Baghdad
